name: Stavropol Krai
summary_text: Stavropol Krai is named in the Canadian travel advisory's special-permission requirement (alongside Chechnya, Dagestan, and Ingushetia) and is included in the North Caucasus zone identified by the UK Home Office CPIN as the exception to Russia's general risk picture. The dossier specifically identifies the south-eastern part bordering Chechnya as subject to the same security-and-custom enforcement logic. However, Stavropol is a krai, not a republic, and the extreme documented violence (secret prisons, purges, coerced conscription) is Chechen-specific rather than krai-wide. For a visitor, the special-permission regime itself restricts movement and independent oversight, and the south-eastern areas adjacent to Chechnya share the localised security culture. The deviation from national (0.12) is approximately 0.05 below. Above the core North Caucasus republics (Dagestan, Ingushetia at 0.04; Kabardino-Balkaria, Karachay-Cherkessia, North Ossetia at 0.05) because the extreme evidence is geographically limited to the Chechnya border zone within a large multi-ethnic krai, and no independent republic-level security apparatus analogous to Kadyrov's exists.

sources.title: Country policy and information note: sexual orientation and gender identity and expression, June 2025 (accessible) - GOV.UK
sources.claim_summary: NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (GOV.UK returned only a cookie-consent shell); the underlying document is the UK Home Office Country Policy and Information Note on sexual orientation and gender identity/expression (June 2025), which concludes that LGBT+ people form a particular social group but that, while sexual minorities generally do not face a real risk of state persecution in Russia, those in the North Caucasus, trans people and publicly active LGBT+ advocates are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution.

sources.title: “Every year it gets worse” – Protecting LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus - Human Rights House Foundation
sources.claim_summary: Interview on the Human Rights House Foundation site with David Isteev of North Caucasus SOS on protecting LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus: 'there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus, and even private existence can trigger violence, detention, or forced return to families'; the organisation coordinates roughly 34 evacuations a year from exile, with security consultations, legal and psychological support and temporary solutions for those who stay.
